Scientists propose using Cold War era weapons to deflect asteroids
ICBMs? Intercepting an object in deep space is quite different from doing it in low Earth orbit that an ICBM can reach.

Bollocks. If there are not other options, then yes, using explosives is better than waiting for the fireworks.

First of all is accuracy. Finding an asteroid that is far away decreases the accuracy in the projection of its orbit. Add to that, the travel time of the missile. If the asteroid is closer, the higher the yield that will be necessary to make a significant enough of an orbital adjustment. Even then there will be a serious lack of information as to the location on the asteroid you want to hit so that subsequent orbits don't put Earth into jeopardy once again. That also assumes the missile will even be able to hit the desired location because there won't be any interstellar guidance. So on one hand, you can try turning the missile into a deep space dumbfire on a distant target with poor knowledge of its trajectory and hope it hits and hope it deflects into a desired orbit. On the other hand, you can try turning the missile into a deep space dumbfire on a close target and hope the explosive yield doesn't break it apart. If it does break up, congratulations, all you've done is spread the asteroid's destructive power over a larger area of the Earth. The explosion won't remove enough mass to make a difference in the asteroid's lethality.

Secondly, without serious research, you won't know for sure what the asteroid consists of, how dense is, what consists of its core, or what consists of its exterior. All of which would inform the location on the asteroid in which to strike with the missile, aside from the issues with missile accuracy. It would also inform you of the limits of the yield so that the exterior isn't completely blown off. If it is blown off, congratulations, you've turned whatever's left into a sabot.

Those are just the first big issues that come to mind. There are only a couple of realistic options to avoid potentially hazardous asteroids although all of them require detecting the astroids as far in advance of a possible impact as possible. In order to do so, more investment in astronomy and space programs is necessary in order to detect the hazardous asteroids early enough to make the trajectory changes. If I remember correctly, it is estimated that only about 25% of potentially hazardous asteroids have been found and their trajectories calculated. That estimated 25% comes to roughly 1700 asteroids. That obviously can't include asteroids that have extreme orbits that fall outside of mankind's history of recording the skies nor can it include asteroids that get nudged and fall into their first near Earth orbit.

The article mentions the use of lasers to create asteroid surface outgassing as a means to nudge the asteroid but that requires a lot of time previous to the possible impact so that the small nudging can translate to a large enough change in trajectory. Another method would be to launch a large mass with attitue adjustment rockets and position it near the asteroid. The asteroid and the launched mass would slowly fall towards each other due to gravity while the rockets keep the launched mass in position. Again, this is small nudging that requires a lot of time to translate to a significant enough change in trajectory. Yet another method would be to land extremely long burn time rockets on the surface of the asteroid and use those rockets to, literally, push the asteroid off course. All of these don't require extensive research investment on the particular astroid's composition to be effective. All of these have the potential to apply more force to the change in trajectory than an ICBM, albeit on a much longer time span.

Sixty five million years ago, if the dinosars had well funded space programs they could have deflected the asteroid that killed them. If they had advanced space programs they could have also moved at least some of their species off the Earth and onto other planets or other star systems. The dinosarus didn't have the brain capacity to science their way out of becoming extinct. Humans do. The problem for us, currently, is that humans are just as susceptible to extinction as the dinosaus. It is not a matter of if but when Earth will have another extinction level asteroid impact. Question is, will humans be ready for it?
